passages.text_new: Theo spent two days gluing foil stars and ribbons onto his kite. It rose, wobbled, and dove into the grass. His cousin Ada's plain paper kite climbed steadily. The wind was the same for both, so Theo stopped blaming it and watched. Ada's kite carried nothing extra except a long, light tail that kept its nose up. Theo pulled off the stars and ribbons and tied on a tail of folded paper bows. His kite lifted and flew. He kept one small ribbon on the handle, where its weight meant nothing to the sky, and decided to test his next kite before decorating it.

passages.text_new: A limestone cave is not carved by one storm or earthquake. Most begin with rain. Rainwater sinking through soil collects a little carbon dioxide, making it slightly acidic. This water seeps into cracks in limestone and dissolves tiny bits of rock; over thousands of years, the cracks widen into tunnels and rooms. Even then, the water keeps working. Each drop falling from the ceiling leaves a speck of mineral, and the specks slowly build stone icicles called stalactites. Visitors see rock that looks finished, yet every tunnel is the sum of tiny changes.

passages.text_old_prefix: [S1] Before the first permanent bridge crossed Bellwater River, ferries carried
passages.text_new: [S1] Before the first permanent bridge crossed Silverbend River, ferries carried people, animals, and supplies between the two banks. [S2] Because the river bent sharply, a boat waiting at one landing could not see whether passengers had gathered at the other. [S3] In 1872, the ferry keeper and a shop owner created a simple signal: a red square raised on a pole meant that passengers were waiting, while a white square meant that freight needed space. [S4] The flags did not tell the ferryman exactly how many people or crates were present, but they helped him decide which boat to send. [S5] During fog, the system failed because neither bank could see the opposite pole, so workers rang a bell in agreed patterns instead. [S6] Old account books show fewer unnecessary crossings after the signals began. [S7] When a bridge finally opened, the flags disappeared, yet the idea behind them remained familiar: send only the information needed for the next decision.

Lesson: how well something works can matter more than how it looks.
